# Motion Design: Web: CSS, Web Animations API & View Transitions

Self-contained. The skill's rules, then this topic, then anything it relies on from other skills.

## Skill rules

Motion is the only design property that exists in time. A bad animation isn't reliably wrong the way a bad color is. It can look fine in isolation and fail only when someone interrupts it mid-flight, drags against it, or triggers it twice in a row. This is the API detail for getting it right on each platform, and the home of the motion tokens.

### Rules That Always Apply

1. **Every animation has a behavioral purpose.** It answers *Where did that go? What just happened? What can I do next?* If it answers none of them, remove it.
2. **Motion values come from the design.** If a spring, curve, or duration isn't specified, ask. The tokens are what you ask with. They're not permission to invent motion.
3. **Native APIs first.** CSS and the Web Animations API, SwiftUI animation modifiers, Compose `animate*` APIs. On web, GSAP is my standard once the work needs timeline choreography, pinning, or scrubbed multi-element scroll. Lenis for smooth scrolling. Three.js for GPU visuals.
4. **Timing functions are named tokens.** No inline `cubic-bezier()`, bare duration, or spring constant at a call site. A token is the only way a motion language stays consistent and gets retuned in one place.
5. **Springs for user-triggered motion, ease curves for system-triggered motion.** The reason is below.
6. **Never linear for UI transitions.** Linear is right in exactly two places: continuous loops, and scroll-linked animation, where scroll position is the clock and any easing fights the user's finger.
7. **Honor reduced motion on every platform.** Replace spatial motion with a fade or an instant change. Don't remove the feedback itself.

### Spring vs. Ease: The Only Decision That Matters

A duration-based curve is mapped to a fixed time window. Interrupt it halfway and the next animation starts from rest. The velocity breaks and the motion visibly jerks.

A spring is defined by physical properties and has no fixed duration. It resolves when it reaches the target. Interrupted mid-flight, it keeps its velocity and carries on. That's why springs feel natural: they behave like objects with momentum.

**Use a spring for anything triggered by user interaction**: taps, drags, swipes, press states, gesture release. **Use an ease curve for anything automated**: loading states, progress indicators, ambient animation, anything that plays without user input. That one rule settles nearly every "spring or ease" question.

On web, CSS has spring-shaped easing (`linear()`), not spring physics. An interrupted CSS transition retargets from the current value but drops the velocity. That's fine for taps and hovers. For drag release or anything thrown, drive the value from JavaScript.

### The Tokens

Names only. Values and per-platform definitions are in [reference/cross-platform-tokens.md](cross-platform-tokens.md).

```
Springs     snappy · standard · expressive · dragRelease
Durations   micro · fast · standard · slow · cinematic
Easings     enter · exit · standard · emphasized · expo-out · sine-in-out
```

Nothing longer than 700ms in product UI. If an animation needs longer than that to feel right, the design problem isn't solved by more motion.

### When Not to Animate

Don't animate when it adds latency to a task, when it's purely decorative, or when it competes with content. A 300ms transition on a frequent action is a regression, not polish.

### Choosing the Web Layer

Work down this list and stop at the first layer that can express the motion. Each step down costs bundle size and main-thread work.

1. **CSS transition or keyframe animation** -- state changes, entrances and exits, hover and press, scroll-linked reveals and progress, page and shared-element transitions.
2. **Web Animations API** -- the same animations when JavaScript must start, reverse, seek, or await them.
3. **GSAP** -- sequenced multi-element timelines, pinning, scrubbed timelines across many elements, text splitting, FLIP layout transitions.
4. **Lenis** -- only when the design calls for smoothed wheel scrolling. It changes how the whole page feels. Never a default.
5. **Three.js** -- when the visual itself needs the GPU: 3D, shaders, particles, post-processing.

## Topic

CSS comes first for web motion. `transform`, `opacity`, and `filter` can animate on the compositor and stay smooth while the main thread is busy. GSAP ([gsap.md](gsap.md)) is for timeline choreography, pinning, and text splitting. Nothing else.

Every sample uses the tokens from [cross-platform-tokens.md](cross-platform-tokens.md#definitions-per-platform): `--duration-*`, `--ease-*`, `--spring-*`, `--motion-distance-*`. That `:root` block is the only place a curve or duration literal appears.

### Status

Support status lives in `web-platform/reference/browser-compatibility.md`. Check it before shipping. What these samples depend on, as of November 2026:

- **Safe everywhere:** `linear()`, individual transform properties, Web Animations API, `@starting-style` entrances, same-document View Transitions.
- **New in one engine, keep the fallback:** scroll-driven animations (Baseline since 2026-10; Firefox only just shipped them).
- **Enhancement only:** animated exits via `display` (no Firefox), `overlay` and `interpolate-size` (Chromium), cross-document View Transitions (no Firefox). The page has to be correct without them, just less animated.

### Transitions

```css
.reveal {
    opacity: 0;
    translate: 0 var(--motion-distance-md);
    transition:
        translate var(--duration-slow) var(--ease-enter),
        opacity var(--duration-standard) var(--ease-enter);
}
.reveal.visible {
    opacity: 1;
    translate: 0 0;
}
```

The individual `translate`, `scale`, and `rotate` properties composite exactly like `transform` and let each take its own duration and curve.

Don't transition `width`, `height`, `top`, `left`, `margin`, `padding`, or `border-width`. They trigger layout every frame. For layout changes use a View Transition, FLIP ([gsap.md](gsap.md#flip-animations)), or the intrinsic-size techniques below. Don't leave `will-change` on permanently. It holds a layer's memory for as long as it applies, and the browser already promotes an element while it animates.

### Springs with linear()

CSS has no spring physics, but `linear()` takes any number of stops, so a spring's response can be sampled into one. That's what the `--spring-*` tokens are.

```css
.button {
    transition: scale var(--spring-snappy-duration) var(--spring-snappy);
}
.button:active {
    scale: 0.97;
}
```

Two limits:

- **It's a spring's shape, not a spring.** The curve assumes a start from rest. An interrupted transition restarts from the current value with zero velocity. For taps, hovers, toggles, and menus you can't tell it from a real spring. For drag release, flings, or anything that inherits gesture velocity, compute the spring in JavaScript per frame.
- **A curve is only valid at its paired duration.** Stretch `--spring-expressive` over two seconds and you get a slow wobble, not a softer spring. A different feel is a new token with new spring parameters, defined in the tokens file.

### Entry and Exit

`@starting-style` gives an element a "before" state the first time it renders or leaves `display: none`, so entrances need no JavaScript.

```css
.toast {
    opacity: 1;
    translate: 0 0;
    transition:
        opacity var(--duration-standard) var(--ease-enter),
        translate var(--duration-standard) var(--ease-enter);

    @starting-style {
        opacity: 0;
        translate: 0 var(--motion-distance-sm);
    }
}
```

Exits need the element to stay rendered until the transition ends. `allow-discrete` lets `display` take part so it flips at the end, and `overlay` keeps a popover or dialog in the top layer meanwhile:

```css
.popover {
    opacity: 0;
    transition:
        opacity var(--duration-fast) var(--ease-exit),
        display var(--duration-fast) allow-discrete,
        overlay var(--duration-fast) allow-discrete;
}
.popover:popover-open {
    opacity: 1;
    transition-timing-function: var(--ease-enter);

    @starting-style {
        opacity: 0;
    }
}
```

Where exits aren't supported the element disappears immediately. That's fine. Don't add JavaScript just to animate an exit.

### Animating to Intrinsic Size

Opening a disclosure to `height: auto` has no transform equivalent.

```css
/* Works everywhere: animate a grid track from 0fr to 1fr */
.disclosure {
    display: grid;
    grid-template-rows: 0fr;
    transition: grid-template-rows var(--duration-standard) var(--ease-standard);
}
.disclosure[data-open="true"] {
    grid-template-rows: 1fr;
}
.disclosure > .content {
    overflow: hidden;
    min-height: 0;
}

/* Chromium enhancement: lets height transition to and from auto */
:root {
    interpolate-size: allow-keywords;
}
```

Both animate layout, so keep them to small regions.

### Web Animations API

When JavaScript has to start, reverse, seek, or await an animation, use `element.animate()` before a library. It runs the same compositor-backed animations and reads the same tokens.

```javascript
const rootStyle = getComputedStyle(document.documentElement);
const token = (name) => rootStyle.getPropertyValue(name).trim();

async function dismiss(card) {
    const animation = card.animate(
        { opacity: [1, 0], translate: ["0 0", `0 ${token("--motion-distance-sm")}`] },
        {
            duration: parseFloat(token("--duration-fast")),
            easing: token("--ease-exit"),
            fill: "forwards"
        }
    );
    await animation.finished;
    card.remove();
}
```

`reverse()`, `playbackRate`, and `currentTime` cover interruption and scrubbing. If the element stays in the DOM, call `commitStyles()` then `cancel()`. Don't leave a `fill: "forwards"` animation holding styles.

### Scroll-Driven Animations

No JavaScript, and `transform`/`opacity` keyframes run on the compositor. Use them for scroll progress, reveal-on-enter, and single-element parallax. Move to GSAP ScrollTrigger when a section has to pin or one scrubbed timeline choreographs many elements.

The timing function is `linear` on purpose: scroll position is the clock. Shape the motion with keyframe offsets and `animation-range`.

```css
/* Scroll progress timeline: tied to a scroll container's position */
.progress-bar {
    transform-origin: left;
    animation: grow linear both;
    animation-timeline: scroll(root block);   /* after the shorthand, which resets it */
}
@keyframes grow {
    from { scale: 0 1; }
    to   { scale: 1 1; }
}

/* View timeline: tied to the element's own visibility in the scrollport */
.section-reveal {
    animation: reveal linear both;
    animation-timeline: view();
    animation-range: entry 0% cover 40%;
}
@keyframes reveal {
    from { opacity: 0; translate: 0 var(--motion-distance-md); }
    to   { opacity: 1; translate: 0 0; }
}

/* Named timeline: several elements driven by one scroller */
.scroll-container {
    scroll-timeline: --hero-scroll block;
}
.hero-text {
    animation: fade-out linear both;
    animation-timeline: --hero-scroll;
    animation-range: 0% 30%;
}
@keyframes fade-out {
    to { opacity: 0; }
}
```

For the fallback, ship a base state driven by a class from `IntersectionObserver` and upgrade inside `@supports`.

```css
.animated-element {
    opacity: 0;
    translate: 0 var(--motion-distance-md);
    transition:
        opacity var(--duration-slow) var(--ease-enter),
        translate var(--duration-slow) var(--ease-enter);
}
.animated-element.visible {
    opacity: 1;
    translate: 0 0;
}

@supports (animation-timeline: view()) {
    .animated-element {
        transition: none;
        animation: reveal linear both;
        animation-timeline: view();
        animation-range: entry 0% entry 60%;
    }
}
```

### View Transitions

Same-document transitions start from JavaScript. Cross-document transitions are declared in CSS for multi-page sites. A browser without support just navigates normally.

```javascript
function navigateTo(url) {
    if (!document.startViewTransition) {
        return loadPage(url);
    }
    return document.startViewTransition(() => loadPage(url)).finished;
}
```

```css
/* The default is a root cross-fade. Name an element to morph it between states. */
.hero-image {
    view-transition-name: hero;
}

::view-transition-group(hero) {
    animation-duration: var(--duration-slow);
    animation-timing-function: var(--ease-emphasized);
}
::view-transition-old(root) {
    animation: var(--duration-fast) var(--ease-exit) both fade-out;
}
::view-transition-new(root) {
    animation: var(--duration-standard) var(--ease-enter) both fade-in;
}

@keyframes fade-out { to { opacity: 0; } }
@keyframes fade-in { from { opacity: 0; } }
```

A `view-transition-name` has to be unique among rendered elements at capture time. Two elements sharing one aborts the transition. For lists, give each item its own name with an inline style and style them as a group with `view-transition-class`.

Cross-document:

```css
/* In the CSS of every page that should participate */
@view-transition {
    navigation: auto;
}
```

Both documents have to opt in. The transition only runs for a same-origin navigation with no cross-origin redirect. Back and forward qualify. A new navigation qualifies only when it starts from the page (link, form, script), not from browser UI like the address bar. Reloads never transition. Names and pseudo-elements work exactly as above.

### Reduce Motion (Web)

The policy is in [cross-platform-tokens.md](cross-platform-tokens.md#reduced-motion-policy). In CSS, write spatial motion as an opt-in for users who haven't asked for less. The fade stays for everyone.

```css
.reveal {
    opacity: 0;
    transition: opacity var(--duration-fast) var(--ease-enter);
}
.reveal.visible {
    opacity: 1;
}

@media (prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference) {
    .reveal {
        translate: 0 var(--motion-distance-md);
        transition:
            translate var(--duration-slow) var(--ease-enter),
            opacity var(--duration-standard) var(--ease-enter);
    }
    .reveal.visible {
        translate: 0 0;
    }
}

/* Scroll-linked motion and View Transition movement are removed outright */
@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) {
    .parallax,
    .section-reveal {
        animation: none;
        opacity: 1;
        translate: none;
    }

    ::view-transition-group(*),
    ::view-transition-old(*),
    ::view-transition-new(*) {
        animation: none;
    }

    html {
        scroll-behavior: auto;
    }
}
```

The global reset (`* { animation-duration: 0.01ms !important; ... }`) kills fades and spinners too. Scope it to third-party markup you don't control. It isn't the primary mechanism.

In JavaScript, `window.matchMedia("(prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)")` gives the same answer. Listen for its `change` event, because the user can flip the setting while the page is open. GSAP doesn't read the preference on its own ([gsap.md](gsap.md#reduced-motion)). Lenis does by default.

##### Support Policy

Baseline tracks Chrome, Edge, Firefox and Safari on desktop and mobile. A feature is **newly available** the day the last of them ships it. It's **widely available** 30 months later.

| Status | How to use it |
| --- | --- |
| Widely available | Freely. No fallback, no `@supports`, no polyfill |
| Newly available | Use it. Add a fallback only where a browser a version or two behind would lose function, not polish. A missing entry animation is fine. A menu that renders off-screen isn't |
| Limited | Progressive enhancement only. The page has to work without it |

No polyfills for anything above 95% support. The one polyfill I carry is Temporal.

##### Widely Available

- **CSS:** cascade layers, container size queries and `cq*` units, nesting, `:has()`, `oklch()`/`oklab()`, `color-mix()`, subgrid, `dvh`/`svh`/`lvh`, `linear()` easing, individual `translate`/`scale`/`rotate`, `:focus-visible`, `:user-valid`/`:user-invalid`, `:modal`, `clip-path`, `mix-blend-mode`, scroll snap, `touch-action`, `env()` safe-area insets, `overscroll-behavior: contain`, `@media (hover)` and `(pointer)`, `prefers-reduced-motion`, `prefers-contrast`, `forced-colors`
- **HTML:** `<dialog>`, `inert`, `loading="lazy"`, `<search>`, import maps, AVIF and WebP
- **JS:** `structuredClone`, `Array.fromAsync`, `Object.groupBy`, `Promise.withResolvers`, `AbortSignal.timeout` and `.any`
- **APIs:** Web Animations, ResizeObserver, IntersectionObserver, Pointer Events, WebGL 2, OffscreenCanvas

**Anchor positioning.** The working core (`anchor-name`, `anchor()`, `position-area`, `position-try-fallbacks`, `@position-try`, `anchor-size()`) is in Chrome 125+, Firefox 147+ and Safari 26+. webstatus.dev still lists the group as limited, because the newest initial value (`position-anchor: normal`) only landed in Chrome 151, Firefox 151 and Safari 27. Treat the core as newly available and keep a non-anchored position as the fallback.

**Web Vitals APIs.** `LargestContentfulPaint` and Event Timing `interactionId` are in every engine, so LCP and INP are measurable everywhere. `LayoutShift` (CLS) and Long Animation Frames are Chromium only.

##### Fallback Patterns

Working default outside `@supports`, enhancement inside:

```css
.tooltip {
    position: absolute;
    inset-block-start: 100%;
    inset-inline-start: 0;
}

@supports (position-area: block-end) {
    .tooltip {
        position-anchor: --trigger;
        position-area: block-end span-inline-end;
        inset: auto;
        position-try-fallbacks: flip-block, flip-inline;
    }
}
```

Detect the capability, never the browser:

```javascript
const yieldToMain = () =>
    globalThis.scheduler?.yield?.() ?? new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, 0));
```

##### Interop 2026

The engines' shared focus list for the year. These are about to get more consistent: anchor positioning, container style queries, dialogs and popovers, scroll-driven animations, view transitions, typed `attr()`, `contrast-color()`, custom highlights, `shape()`, scroll snap, the Navigation API and `zoom`, among others. Live pass rates are at wpt.fyi/interop-2026.

##### Testing Checklist

- Chrome, Firefox, Edge: latest and latest-1
- Safari: latest on macOS and on a real iOS device. Every iOS browser is WebKit, and desktop emulation misses its viewport and touch behavior
- Samsung Internet
- One mid-range Android device, real or on a device cloud

Safari is usually the engine holding a feature out of Baseline. Anything in the newly available table gets one manual pass there.
